title: Forced conversions
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE institutional bias against minority females leaves them to either be directly victimised or to live in conditions where mistreatment is their daily reality. The Senate Minority Caucus, following the disappearance of a 14-year-old Hindu girl, has directed law enforcement to recover the victim, and also voiced concern about the abductions, reported forced conversions and marriages of non-Muslim girls in Sindh and Balochistan. While the police chiefs of the two provinces stated that a writ petition had been filed, their claim was denied by a Supreme Court lawyer who added that no serious efforts were made to find her. From highlighting the helplessness of the state and the police when it comes to dealing with an influential pir’s alleged “state within a state” to the need to criminalise these excesses in order to end them, the committee’s observations were not new.   
Chauvinism persists because legislation to proscribe forced conversions was blocked by the right a decade ago. In 2016, the Sindh Assembly did pass a bill stipulating that any conversion by a minor would only come into effect when they attain the age of 18 years, and it also prescribed severe punishments for the perpetrators of forced conversions. The ensuing outrage by the orthodox lobby comprising those accused of playing a key role in these acts compelled the provincial government to cave in. Thus the bill was not signed into law. Politicians have since failed to show any commitment towards pursuing a legal framework to uproot these problematic practices. This does question the intent of the state: does it allow circumstances where condemnable practices continue; where those responsible go scot-free; where the police are often found complicit with powerful offenders? It is high time such acts were seen as crimes of power and control. In a civilised society, deep-seated social prejudice cannot be permitted to strip vulnerable communities of their dignity and liberties.

title: Judicial disaffection
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE resignation of Justice Mohsin Akhtar Kayani from the Lahore High Court is another indicator of the deepening disaffection within Pakistan’s superior judiciary. That a senior judge should feel compelled to relinquish office on grounds of conscience speaks volumes about the conditions prevailing under the new constitutional order. Justice Kayani has cited personal and health reasons, but his criticism of the 26th and 27th Amendments is telling. He believes these changes have compromised the independence of the high courts and strengthened executive control over judicial appointments. His own transfer from the Islamabad High Court to the LHC, which cost him his seniority, provides important context. His departure follows the resignations of Justices Mansoor Ali Shah, Athar Minallah and Shams Mehmood Mirza, who also expressed grave reservations about the constitutional changes. These are experienced judges raising key questions about the judiciary’s ability to function independently. Their concerns cannot simply be dismissed.
Equally important is Justice Kayani’s warning about the ordinary litigant, whose interests, he says, have been neglected. This deserves serious attention. For millions of Pakistanis, approaching the courts already means enduring delays, mounting legal expenses and years of uncertainty. A judiciary whose independence is questioned can only deepen their sense of helplessness. If citizens begin to believe that judicial decisions may be influenced by powerful interests, their faith in obtaining a fair hearing will suffer. The constitutional amendments were defended as measures to improve the administration of justice, yet the growing unease among senior judges raises legitimate doubts about their consequences. The government and judicial leadership must acknowledge these concerns and address them through meaningful institutional dialogue. An independent judiciary is essential to protecting citizens against arbitrary power. When judges themselves question whether that independence can be maintained, the country has reason to worry.
Published in Dawn, October 30th, 2026

title: Moscow’s Afghan outreach
author: none@none.com (Asif Durrani)
content:
RUSSIA’S growing engagement with Afghanistan’s Taliban rulers is reshaping the regional diplomatic landscape. For Pakistan, which has historically maintained close links with Afghan political and religious networks, the development presents both a challenge and an opportunity. The question is not whether Moscow will replace Islamabad as Kabul’s principal interlocutor, but whether Russia’s expanding diplomatic, security and economic engagement will give the Taliban greater room to manoeuvre in their dealings with Pakistan.
Russia’s approach towards the Taliban has been gradually shaping up. In July 2025, Moscow became the first country to recognise the Taliban government formally. Earlier, it announced the removal of the Taliban from its list of prohibited terrorist organisations in April that year. In May 2026, Russian officials announced plans to establish a “full-fledged partnership” with Kabul, encompassing security, trade, cultural exchanges, and humanitarian cooperation. That same month, a military-technical cooperation arrangement further underscored the deepening relationship. Moscow, therefore, has been moving beyond limited diplomatic engagement towards a more sustained relationship with the Taliban authorities. Multiple factors may be shaping Moscow’s approach toward the Taliban.
First, Moscow remains concerned about the spread of militant violence into Central Asia, narcotics trafficking, and the activities of Islamic State-Khorasan (IS-K). The deadly 2024 attack near Moscow reinforced Russian concerns about transnational extremist networks. From the Kremlin’s perspective, dealing with the Taliban is a pragmatic necessity — whatever its reservations about the nature of their government, the Taliban exercise effective control over Afghan­istan’s state institutions and security apparatus.
In parallel, Russia seeks to preserve its influence in Eurasia and prevent Afghanistan from becoming a source of instability that could invite renewed intervention by external powers. Economic cooperation, including potential opportunities in energy, transport, agriculture, and infrastructure, adds another dimension to this policy. Moscow’s outreach should, therefore, be understood as an effort to protect its own interests and expand its regional options.
Russia’s close ties with Kabul won’t automatically ensure action against anti-Pakistan terrorists.
Second, Russia’s recognition of the Taliban has important implications for Pakistan’s diplomatic leverage. For years, Islamabad’s geographical proximity, economic connections, and historical links with the Taliban gave it considerable access to Kabul. Russian recognition gives Kabul an additional source of international legitimacy. Its expanding relations with Moscow also offer the Taliban another channel for diplomatic engagement, security cooperation, and economic opportunity. The more external partners Kabul acqui­res, the less dependent it may feel on Islamabad for diplomatic access and international engagement.
This does not mean that Pakistan’s influence will disappear. Geography, cross-border commerce, people-to-people links, and the management of shared security concerns remain important. However, these factors do not automatically translate into political compliance. Pakistan’s leverage will increasingly depend on whether it can demonstrate the mutual benefits of cooperation rather than rely on historical relationships or geographical realities alone.
Third, Russia’s approach to the TTP will be the most consequential test. Islamabad’s central secu­­rity concern is that terrorist groups operating from Afghan territory threaten Pakistan’s citizens and security personnel. The Taliban authorities’ generalised statement is that Afghan territory will not be used against other countries, but they are reluctant to specifically say that Afghan territory will not be allowed to be used against Pakistan.
Moscow’s priorities, however, do not match Pakistan’s. Russia’s immediate security concerns centre particularly on IS-K and the threat of extremist violence spreading into Central Asia and Russia itself. Although the Taliban also oppose IS-K, this convergence does not necessarily mean Moscow will place Pakistan’s concerns about the TTP at the centre of its Afghan policy.
Pakistan should, therefore, avoid assuming that Russia’s close relations with Kabul will automatically produce action against anti-Pakistan terrorists. Russian influence could provide an additional diplomatic channel, but its effectiveness will depend on Moscow’s willingness to address the TTP issue and the Taliban leadership’s readiness to respond.
Fourth, Russia’s interest in regional stability gives it a potential role in facilitating dialogue, reducing tensions and encouraging practical cooperation. Pakistan should welcome constructive Russian involvement without outsourcing its Afghan policy to Moscow.
The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation could provide a useful multilateral framework. Pakistan, Russia, China, and the Central Asian states share an interest in preventing Afghanistan from becoming a base for transnational terrorism. Coordinated intelligence exchanges, border-security cooperation, counter-narcotics measures, and structured consultations with Kabul could help establish a regional approach. Such cooperation would be more sustainable than expecting any single country to exercise decisive influence over the Taliban.
Fifth, Pakistan needs to adapt its Afghan policy to a more competitive diplomatic environment. Islamabad should deepen engagement with Russia while maintaining direct communication with the Taliban leadership. It should also coordinate with China, the Central Asian republics, and other relevant regional actors to develop a common understanding of the threats emanating from Afghanistan.
At the bilateral level, Pakistan has to involve the Taliban in a meaningful dialogue and create a workable environment that builds the Taliban regime’s stake in the mutual benefits of the two countries. This could include arrangements to exchange information on terrorist networks, investigate cross-border incidents, prevent attacks, and maintain communication between security officials. Economic cooperation and the facilitation of legitimate trade should accompany these measures, giving both sides practical incentives to reduce tensions.
Diplomatically, Russia’s Afghan outreach is thus neither an inevitable strategic setback for Pakistan nor a guarantee of improved regional security. It is a development that reflects the Tali­ban’s efforts to widen their international options and Moscow’s decision to protect its own interests. Whether this produces greater stability or further competition will depend on how regional states use their expanding diplomatic channels.
Pakistan will have to carefully observe that Russia’s engagement helps address the region’s shared security concerns. Islamabad’s influence over Kabul will ultimately depend less on who has the closest relationship with the Taliban and more on who can help produce practical results: a secure border, action against militant violence, functioning trade routes and a stable regional environment.
The writer is a former special representative of Pakistan for Afghanistan. He served as Pakistan’s ambassador to the UAE and Iran.
Published in Dawn, October 29th, 2026

title: A huddle in Tehran
author: none@none.com (Khurram Husain)
content:
LAST month, I argued in this space that Iran is emerging as a big regional power to our west. The question I left hanging was whether it would use its newfound centrality to avenge the past or to build a future. Last week offered the first real glimpse of an answer.
On Oct 26, Saudi Arabia’s defence minister, Pakistan’s defence chief, and Turkiye’s intellige­nce chief sat down in Tehran with Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council. The joint statement that followed was thin, pledging only continued dialogue on regional peace and security. But the significance of the Tehran huddle lies less in what was said than in the fact that it happened at all, and where.
Consider who came. The three visitors are the signatories of the Makkah Joint Defence Agree­m­ent, signed in August, a pact many read as a hedge against precisely the kind of Iran I described last month. Saudi Arabia was struck repeatedly by Iran during the war, hosted American forces that attacked Iran, and is under fire from the Houthis even now. Yet, the Saudi defence minister led the delegation, and they travelled to Tehran. Not Riyadh, Ankara or Islamabad, nor a neutral venue like Doha or Muscat.
    
When three of the region’s largest military powers, one of them nuclear-armed, come to your capital to talk about regional security, they are acknowledging that no regional security arrangement is possible without you, and that the road to one runs through your door. For a country that spent four decades behind a wall of sanctions and was treated as a problem to be contained rather than a party to be consulted, this is a milestone.
The significance of the Tehran huddle lies less in what was said than in the fact that it happened at all, and where.
It also happened in the teeth of American pressure. Washington was openly weighing a fresh round of strikes, US forces were reportedly ready to move within 96 hours of an order, and a naval blockade was choking Iran’s southern ports. The region’s middle powers came anyway, having concluded that Iran would still be standing after this war and that they need a working relationship with it whatever Washington decided.
The second thing worth noticing is what Iran chose to emphasise. Rezaei told state television that Tehran and its three guests had agreed that the region’s security is to be achieved through the countries of the region. A senior Pakistani security official told Reuters the meeting’s primary aim was a regional mechanism to prevent military attacks between them. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said for months that Tehran will welcome any regional security arrangement that excludes foreign forces.
Put these together and the outline of the order Iran wants comes into view. It rests on three pillars: non-aggression among the states of the region, an alignment of their interests, and the exit of outside powers, above all America, from the business of guaranteeing Gulf security.
This is a window into the kind of power Iran wants to project. Last month, I worried that once the Americans were gone, the Iranian military machine would turn its gaze to the riches of the Gulf monarchs and present bill after bill. That risk has not gone away. But the posture on display in Tehran was not that of a power seeking to dominate its neighbours by force. It was that of a power seeking to become the indispensable centre of a regional system it helps design.
The China analogy is instructive here too. In 1954, with Beijing still shunned by much of the world, Zhou Enlai put forward the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence in negotiations with India. Mutual non-aggression sat at their heart, alongside non-interference in internal affairs. Non-aggression is the language of a power confident of its own weight, which wants its neighbours to accommodate it rather than fear it.
There is hard strategic logic beneath the soft language. A non-aggression architecture without foreign forces is the one in which Iran’s advantages count most. Take American bases and carriers out of the Gulf, and Iran’s hold over Hormuz, its missile arsenal, and its network of allies make it the pre-eminent power on the Gulf littoral by default. In that setting, a non-aggression pact is not a concession but a way of having one’s pre-eminence ratified by one’s neighbours.
    
Nor did the idea originate in Tehran. In May, Saudi Arabia itself floated a non-aggression pact between Iran and the states of the region, reportedly modelled on the 1975 Helsinki Accords. Iran is now taking an idea its rivals put on the table and making it the organising principle of an order with itself at the centre. That, too, is what emerging powers do.
None of this is settled. The factional contest I described last month is playing out in plain sight. The hard-line daily Kayhan treated oil above $115 a barrel as proof that pressure on shipping works better than diplomacy, while moderate papers warn of a wave of bankruptcies in Isfahan, Tabriz, and Arak as the blockade bites. Which camp prevails will decide whether the language of non-aggression is here to stay.
Pakistan has a particular stake in all this. An Iran that seeks pre-eminence through a regional architecture is a neighbour Pakistan can work with, and help shape from the inside. An Iran that seeks it through reparations, tolls, and coercion would place us in an impossible position between our western neighbour and the Gulf states on which so much of our economy depends.
The huddle does not answer last month’s question. But it shows that the option of building a future is on the table, in Iran’s own words, and that its neighbours are prepared to engage on those terms. That is a milestone. Whether it becomes a trajectory depends on whether the voices in Teh­ran speaking the language of non-aggression win the argument at home, and whether Washington, after its elections on Nov 3, lets them.
The writer is a business and economy journalist.

title: Polluted priorities
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
LAHORE is choking again, and the government’s answer is to send more machines onto its streets. On Wednesday, its air quality index reached 296, putting children, outdoor workers, and the elderly at particular risk. Yet Punjab plans to acquire 30 more truck-mounted fog cannons. These can suppress road dust locally, but their ability to reduce the fine particles most harmful to health remains questionable. Authorities must explain what the existing fleet has achieved in terms of measurable pollution reduction before spending more public money. Last year, disruptions to Punjab’s air monitoring network raised suspicions that pollution levels were being hidden; officials cited technical faults. Whether equipment is recording pollution or spraying water, public confidence depends on transparent data and independent scrutiny. A temporary improvement at a pollution hotspot, or near a monitoring station, cannot prove that the city’s air is becoming safer. Monitoring should expose pollution. Punjab must publish continuous readings and independent assessments of its interventions. It should also fund research into the relative contributions of traffic, industry, construction, and crop burning, how these change with the seasons, and which measures actually reduce exposure.
That scientific effort must extend beyond the border. Punjab officials say easterly winds have been bringing polluted air from India into Lahore. But this does not absolve Pakistan of responsibility for its own emissions. The air over the two Punjabs is shared, and both populations suffer when political hostility obstructs cooperation. Calls for joint action are not new. Cooperation was proposed with Indian Punjab in 2017 and 2024. Yet neither initiative led to sustained cooperation. Environmental diplomacy with New Delhi should be prioritised, despite wider tensions. Both sides could begin by exchanging verified air-quality and weather data, jointly studying the movement of pollutants and developing common approaches to agricultural burning and industrial emissions. Universities and scientific institutions could help build a shared evidence base. At home, dedicated research funding, stronger monitoring, and open evaluation of anti-smog spending are essential. Enforcement must continue, but decisions should follow evidence, not the visibility of machinery on city roads. Until the air itself improves, no amount of official activity can be called progress.

title: From such seeds
author: none@none.com (F.S. Aijazuddin)
content:
ON Nov 3 this year, Aitchison College, Lahore, will celebrate its 140th birthday. It has outlived the former Indian Civil Service which lasted 87 years (1858-1947), and is almost twice the age of the ICS’ successor, the Pakistan Civil Service.
In many ways, the path and purpose of Aitchison College have run parallel to both, in that it has produced generations of pre- and post-independence leadership.
At the time of independence, in August 1947, there were 980 ICS officers. They comprised 468 British and 512 Indian locals. Of the latter, 352 were Hindus and 101 Muslims. The remainder were a smattering of other faiths. The first Indian to be admitted to the ICS was Satyendranath Tagore, in 1863.
Until the 1950s, the ICS remained a misogynist preserve, as Aitchison College is even today. The first woman to be admitted into the Indian Administrative Service (IAS) was Anna Rajam Malhotra, who joined its 1951 batch. Initially, the Union Public Service Commission Board after her viva voce interview tried to discourage her from joining the IAS. It offered her the Foreign Service and Cen­tral Services, because these were ‘more suitable for women’. She resisted their blandishments, and in time rose in her career to become India’s first secretary.
Between 1950 and 2020, out of 11,569 officers who entered the IAS, only 1,527 (roughly 13 per cent) were women. The gender imbalance has been corrected since. The 2024 batch contained 41pc women.
That is lower than the counterpart representation in Pakistan’s civil service where, out of 217 fresh entrants into the 54th Common Training Programme (2026), 117 were men and almost half (100) women. Some of them will rise (male prejudice notwithstanding) to become secretaries in the federal government, as once the brave and unsung Miss Gulzar Bano had done.
In November 1947, Miss Gulzar Bano and her nine younger siblings travelled without their parents from Lucknow to Lahore. All she carried with her was a slip of paper containing the address of a relative living in Model Town. She studied with diligence, often attending school on alternate days as she and her sister had to share the same pair of shoes. In 1950, she sat for the CSS examination, topping the list of successful candidates. After the viva voce, however, the selection board relega­ted her to the second position because “it lacked confidence in women’s talents”.
She suffered a second humiliation when she discovered that she could not join the ‘serious’ services — the CSP, Foreign Service, or the Police. She had to join the Audit and Accounts Service. She reported to the accountant general (Post and Telegraph), who arranged for her desk to be placed in the public hall near the superintendent (her junior). The office had no toilet for ladies. On occasions, she was forced “to take a tonga to Government College” to relieve herself.
She reached the top of the bureaucracy’s greasy pole when she became cabinet secretary for a brief period, from June 4 to Dec 14, 1978. She described her 30-year career as a “kind of loneliness which only a single Pakistani woman starting work in the 1950s” could understand.
Ms Bano would have been gratified to learn that her example has inspired many women. Ms Tehmina Janjua, for one. In February 2017, she became our first female foreign secretary.
Such gender calibration suggests there is hope, were it not for the dismal results of the civil service exams. The results of the CSS 2026 written exam provide grim reading. Out of 17,351 candidates who ap­­p­eared, only 476 candidates qualified, with a pass rate of 2.7pc. (Incidentally, 239 were men and 237 women.) For de­­tails of their results, one is referred by the Federal Public Service Commission to its results portal. Access it, and you will get this message: “No active information available in this section.”The FPSC has itself become a role model of institutionalised inertia.
Aspirants to our civil service undoubtedly study hard, pore over articles, digest numerous books, and plough through exam guides. But obviously, that is not enough. They may read everything, yet they learn nothing.
Had they been Chinese, they would have had to memorise between 50,000 to 100,000 characters. As it is, some of our senior civil servants, aspiring to be promoted to the level of federal secretaries, have found difficulty in mastering even 26 letters in the English alphabet. Some still think the title of the founder of our nation is ‘Quad-e-Azam’ or ‘Quid-e-Azam’.
One is reminded of the senior student at Aitchison College who concluded his recitation of a story once with the innovative word: ‘Theend’.
From such seeds…
The writer is an author.

title: Elusive quality
author: none@none.com (Shahzad Sharjeel)
content:
EACH year, the noise grows louder and the naming and shaming of public entities reaches its crescendo around budget time. The music sheet remains unchanged, the chorus: ‘cuts in development allocations in the social sectors’. ‘Cacophony’ is a better descriptor. However, what adds insult to injury is that, in keeping with tradition, the health and education ministries have failed to fully utilise even the minuscule allocations they received in the outgoing fiscal year, prompting the Planning Commission to admonish them and donors to protest yet another set of rollover requests from the relevant departments.
The development fraternity continues to lament that whatever little is allocated to human development mostly falls under the non-development or recurrent category, and very little, if anything, is left for ‘development’. While successive governments have not overcome the fiscal constraints, real or imagined, in increasing budget allocations to the social sector, the public discourse has also not risen beyond hackneyed criticism.
Isn’t it time to ask, recurrent as they may be, why salaries in the education department are considered beyond the pale of development? Yes, the proportion of administrative versus teaching cadres must be debated, but the debate should also expand to include questions such as, ‘what about monitoring and evaluation?’, ‘what about coaching support for teachers?’, ‘what about assessment systems for students and teachers?’
True, AI will play a role, but trained, mo­­tivated human resources can’t be ign­ored. Salaries and career trajectories that attract the country’s best talent must be considered as much a part of development as curricula, textbook content and design, learning aids, and training. The less said about civil works the better. Infrastructure is essential to ensure a safe, conducive learning environment, but boundary walls and rooms alone won’t foster learning outcomes, critical thinking, and problem-solving abilities among students.
Education quality can’t improve without quality expenditure.
Education quality can’t improve without quality expenditure. No rocket science; it’s just another way of saying ‘bang for the buck’ or stretching the rupee. A low-fee private school in a small building with little to no space for physical training or sports still enjoys more parental trust than a large public school next door with some, if not all, facilities, even though it pays a fraction of the salary a public-sector teacher earns and provides almost no training. While one cannot regulate private schools beyond preventing exploitation, public school teachers can surely be supported to produce better learning outcomes for students. In the next phase, non-performers should be removed.
While discussing the quality of expenditure, when was the last time we heard of an independent audit of teacher recruitment, training, and coaching mechanisms in the public sector? What incentives are in place for those who perform well, and what disincentives can be implemented under the current lifelong job guarantee, which is assumed not only by teachers but also the judicial system? Try denying an erring teacher a promotion they believe their years of service warrant, or firing an egregious one, and the courts will issue a stay order and then revoke any proposed disciplinary action, with full payment of arrears accrued during the litigation.
We can create as many islands of excellence in this sea of inequity as we like, but we can’t address what ails our education until we adopt a systemic, holistic, and transformative approach to reform. This calls for collective leadership, with the choir led by the very children whose futures are at stake, and with the voices of their parents and communities heard.
People change systems. People must exercise their agency and stop vo­­ting for transfers and postings, or for petty dispu­te resolution at the revenue department or police station level. They must demand that party manifestos specifically address issues with far-reaching impact on future generations, and then hold their representatives, whether in the ruling alliance or in opposition, accountable. Responsive governance and politics require compromise; only a collective of citizens can ensure that these trade-offs benefit future generations rather than private gain.
While the enigma of what truly guarantees national sovereignty is unresolved, the demand for increased human development allocations must be paired with insistence on expenditure quality to ensure development effectiveness. A matriculate able to read, comprehend, and calculate at a level commensurate with 10 years of schooling is not too much to ask. If this cannot be achieved, budgets, whether recurrent or developmental, yield nothing but deficits.
The writer is a poet. His latest publication is a collection of satire essays titled Rindana.

title: Restructuring plans
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE PPP appears quite perturbed over the fact that the creation of new provinces or administrative units continues to be discussed. Speaking at an event in Karachi on Tuesday, PPP chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari asserted that no one outside Sindh could decide its future. “So we should now put a full stop to this conversation as well.” The Bhutto scion said the people of Sindh and their elected representatives had “given their verdict” on this matter, ostensibly referring to a Sindh Assembly resolution in early September. Solely on principle, his position cannot be faulted. The Constitution does lay out a clear process for decisions of this sort, and it gives the elected assembly of each affected province a final say on the matter. Of course, there are public representatives from the same province, albeit from other parties, who disagree with the PPP chairperson’s view. However, that disagreement alone cannot be used to override a defined legal process.
Unfortunately, as recent events in KP have shown, the public’s mandate and verdicts delivered through the ballot box can be brushed aside if the centre is sufficiently motivated. For KP, its decisions are now being made not by its elected representatives, but by administrators handpicked by Islamabad. It can be argued that this is, perhaps, not a fair comparison, but Mr Bhutto-Zardari should still realise that his position may not hold as much force as he thinks it does, and it will, therefore, not be as easy to bury this agenda as he would like. There are many voices within the federal government’s ruling coalition that are actively advocating for the division of all provinces into more ‘manageable’ units. As was seen in KP, such voices can be amplified to find causa proxima, the trigger for an intervention, if it comes to that. Therefore, a better course of action would be to address governance grievances proactively.
The primary reason for governance failure in Pakistan is not the geographical size of the existing provinces but the reluctance of provincial capitals to empower local bodies. Few can convincingly argue that the local government system, as it exists today, is capable of positive change at the grassroots level. At the same time, simply creating more provinces will only add heavy, expensive layers of provincial bureaucracy at a time when Pakistan can ill afford them. There are also steep social costs to consider, as pushing forward without public validation could trigger ethnic strife. Therefore, empowered local bodies remain the best answer to all those issues which seem to warrant a fracturing of the provinces in the eyes of those demanding an administrative restructuring. The decrepit LG system needs to be revitalised, with resources invested in it judiciously. Doing so can improve service delivery at the neighbourhood level in a meaningful way.

title: Constitutional questions
author: none@none.com (Khwaja Ahmad Hosain)
content:
PAKISTAN has had three constitutions. Two given to it by its people in 1956 and 1973. One promulgated by a field marshal in 1962. The 1973 Constitution was adopted by the people through their representatives in the constituent assembly. Article 1 states that Pakistan shall be a federal republic. Neither the term “federal” nor “republic” is expressly defined. The Objectives Resolution provides guidance.
The power and authority of the state in our republic is to be exercised through the chosen representatives of the people. A republic is distinct from rule by one man. In a republic, rulers are not immune from accountability. They can be removed and replaced if they fail to perform.
The various territories that are part of Pakistan or that accede to Pakistan form a federation. These territories are autonomous and their boundaries and powers and authority are prescribed. The Objectives Resolution guarantees that the integrity of the territories shall be safeguarded.
A federal state is brought into being by the territories that comprise it through a written instrument. This instrument defines the authority of the federation and these territories. The federation presupposes and is premised on the existence of these territories. Dismantling the territories would undermine the foundational integrity of the federation and the compact reflected in the 1973 Constitution.
    
A constitution can be amended. The limits of a province or territory can be changed with its consent. Such an amendment may alter limits or provincial boundaries. It does not contemplate partition or subdivision of existing provinces or existing territories. Actions that compromise provincial integrity inevitably lead to questions regarding the benefits of being part of the federation. These questions have been resolved by the various territories and reflected in the 1973 Constitution. It would not be wise to reopen them.
Emergency powers cannot be used to deprive any citizen of the right to a fair trial.
Provincial integrity is not incompatible with devolution of power and effective local government. The Principles of Policy of the Constitution require the state to encourage local government institutions. Each province is constitutionally required to establish a local government system and to devolve power.
The president is the head of state and represents the unity of the republic. The president as a symbol of a united federation must be satisfied prior to provincial autonomy being assailed. This can only be done in exceptional circumstances. The emergency provisions enable federal rule over a province if the president is satisfied that certain conditions exist.
The president does not have authority to impo­­se an emergency whenever he deems fit. The eme­rgency provisions are not like the erstwhile Arti­cle 58(2)(b). The president was empowered under this Article to dissolve an elected government in his discretion. The emergency powers are not exp­ressed to be discretionary powers of the president.
Could the president have refused to sign the recent emergency proclamation notwithstanding the advice of the federal government? He could certainly have asked the government to look at matters again. Did he have discretion to refuse if after reconsideration the government insisted?
The term “discretion” is not used in the relevant Articles of the Constitution. The conventional legal view is that absent a power being expressed as discretionary, the president is bound to act on the advice of the government. In the case of the emergency provisions the president is required to be “satisfied”. This suggests a mental state of an individual office holder.
It could be argued that a mental state cannot be imposed through governmental advice. Regardless, in the present emergency, this appears to be a moot point since the president did not even ask the government to re­­c­onsider its advice. We do not know the nature of the material made available to the president to satisfy him beyond what is contained in the proclamation. Its contents are in substance assertions and non-speaking. They do not provide cogent reasons.
If the stipulated conditions for an emergency do not exist, the proclamation is unlawful. It is incorrect to state that because emergency powers exist in the Constitution, the exercise thereof is constitutional. The existence of a power and its lawful exercise are two distinct matters.
    
Emergency powers cannot be used to deprive any citizen of Pakistan of the right to a fair trial. The emergency provisions enable suspension of operation of a provision of the Constitution only relating to a body or authority in the province. They do not permit the suspension of Article 10-A of the Constitution which provides for a fair trial and due process. The federal government’s order pursuant to the proclamation states that Article 175(3) shall not apply to the designated districts. This Article provides for separation of the judiciary from the executive. The constitutional framework does not contemplate such suspension.
The emergency provisions also do not authorise the subdivision of a province by creating a separate governance structure for certain designated parts absent provincial legislative consent. Where certain federally administered areas have been made part of a province through a constitutional amendment (as is the case with Fata), the impact of this amendment cannot lawfully be undone through a proclamation of emergency which is an executive action.
Depriving people of a territory of rule by their representatives is undemocratic and diminishes the federation. When imposed on an unwilling provincial government, it pits the centre against one of its parts and weakens the whole. Normal constitutional functioning should be restored as soon as possible.
The real question that needs consideration is whether currently Pakistan is truly operating as a federal republic. That is what is contemplated by the first Article of our Constitution. If the compact that binds the territories that comprise our nation is broken, what credible vision can the rulers offer the people in these territories? The existential challenge the country faces is not from its enemies and those who wish us ill. It is from power being divorced from political authority and therefore accountability. That is the real emergency facing us. Until we confront this truth, the story of Pakistan will not change.
The writer is a lawyer.
Published in Dawn, October 28th, 2026

title: AI’s brain & muscle
author: none@none.com (Nazir A. Jogezai)
content:
ARTIFICIAL intelligence is usually presented as weightless, almost entirely digital. We ask it to write, calculate, translate or create an image, and the response appears instantly. Yet every answer depends on a substantial physical system. This comprises data centres, specialised processors, cooling equipment etc.
In reality AI has both ‘brain’ and ‘muscle’. Algorithms, software, researchers, engineers and companies comprise its brain. Its muscle consists of electricity, computing infrastructure, minerals, manufacturing capacity and reliable networks. The first phase of global AI competition focused mainly on the brain. As AI becomes more widely used, the muscle is becoming impossible to ignore.
    
The International Energy Agency expects electricity demand from data centres to more than double by 2030, with AI a major driver. The challenge is not simply producing more power. It is producing reliable electricity supply and expanded transmission networks to accommodate the needs of large data centres. Oil and gas reserves beneath the ground are not the same as electricity delivered to a data centre. Resources become strategic only when they can be converted into dependable infrastructure.
The physical foundations of AI also include copper, aluminium, silicon, and rare-earth materials. Advanced semiconductor technologies depend on specialised materials, while mining and refining remain concentrated in a limited number of countries. The digital economy has not escaped geography! An algorithm can cross a border in milliseconds, but a power plant, mine or factory cannot.
This creates a new geopolitical equation. Countries with the strongest AI research and software ecosystems may still depend on others for energy, minerals and manufacturing. Resource-rich countries, meanwhile, may possess the muscle of the AI economy without the universities, capital, software and semiconductor capabilities needed to turn it into computing power. The long-term advantage may belong to countries that can connect the two.
The digital economy has not escaped geography.
    
Pakistan illustrates this challenge clearly. It is not currently a leading frontier-AI power and faces serious constraints in reliable electricity, advanced computing, research funding etc. Yet it has a large young population, growing software and IT-services sectors, universities, engineering talent, hydropower and renewable-energy potential, and significant mineral resources. The strategic challenge is therefore not simply to acquire more resources or develop more algorithms, but to connect the country’s physical assets with its scientific and technological capabilities.
That would require moving beyond traditional models of exporting raw materials and low-value services. An AI-era strategy would use reliable energy, connectivity and mineral resources to support data centres, cloud services, local research, advanced applications and value-added manufacturing. AI could strengthen sectors such as agriculture, textiles, logistics, mining, health, education and public administration. In this model, AI becomes an industrial multiplier rather than merely another software sector.
Resource wealth alone, however, guarantees neither technological independence nor prosperity. Natural resources cannot substitute for universities, skilled workers, capital, innovation and capable institutions. The relationship between AI’s brain and muscle is better understood as multiplication rather than addition. A country with excellent algorithms but unreliable power will struggle to scale, while a country with abundant energy but weak research capacity may remain a commodity supplier.
The lesson extends beyond Pakistan. Countries such as the United States have ex­­traordinary stren­gths in research, capital, technology companies and advanced computing. China combines rapidly advancing AI with industrial scale and manufacturing capacity. Gulf countries possess energy and capital, while Australia and Canada have substantial mineral and energy advantages.
None controls every part of the AI system. Interdependence will remain unavoidable, but countries that connect more stages, from energy and minerals to computing and applications, will have greater strategic influence.
For Pakistan and other natural resource-rich countries, the message is immediate. An AI strategy cannot stop at applications, start-ups or policy statements. It must also address reliable electricity, data-centre infrastructure, digital skills, research institutions, mineral value addition and industrial capacity.
The next phase of the AI race will not be decided solely by who builds the smartest models. It will also be decided by who can power them, supply them and apply them productively. AI has a brain. But without muscle, even the most brilliant brain cannot move.
The writer is an educationist.
Published in Dawn, October 28th, 2026

title: The Tehran opening
author: none@none.com (Zahid Hussain)
content:
HELD amid the threat of a renewed US-Israeli attack on Iran and escalating conflict in the Arabian Peninsula, the meeting between Iranian leaders and members of the Makkah Defence Alliance was deeply significant — though it remained unclear whether the talks had produced any major breakthrough. The quadrilateral meeting reportedly discussed “regional cooperation, the US-Israeli aggression against Iran and its consequences”, among other topics.
It was the first high-level contact between Iran and all of the alliance’s members since Saudi Arabia was drawn deeper into its conflict with the Houthis. The gathering came days after a brief visit to Tehran by Pakistan’s army chief, during which he reportedly proposed the meeting — a suggestion Iranian leaders responded to positively.
    
That visit was essentially a part of Pakistan’s mediatory efforts to restart the stalled peace talks between America and Iran, and a response to the latest flare-up in the region. Since the collapse of a brief ceasefire reached in April, the United States has imposed an economic blockade on Iran in an attempt to force it to capitulate. It has not. Iran has kept control of the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas used to flow.
The diplomatic efforts of Pakistan and Qatar have so far failed to break the stalemate. The main stumbling block to resuming peace talks has been President Trump’s insistence that Iran give up its enriched uranium stockpile. Iran has refused, insisting that the US must end its naval blockade and start negotiations on the seven points that overlap with the Islamabad memorandum of understanding. Iranian leaders have repeatedly declared that “not a single particle of enriched nuclear material” would leave Iran.
Regional peace can be ensured only through a regional security architecture.
Tensions rose further with reports of a possible joint US-Israeli attack on Iran before the US midterm elections. According to American media, Israel had been pressing Trump to resume airstrikes before Israel’s own general elections, which were held yesterday. There are still indications that Trump could restart military action after the American midterms on Nov 3.
Iranian officials warned last week that if Iran were attacked again, its forces would widen their targets to data centres and underwater internet cables in the region.
The situation has grown more volatile with the escalation of the Saudi-Houthi conflict. The Yemeni rebel group, which now controls a large part of the country and Bab al-Mandeb, a critical chokepoint on the Red Sea, has repeatedly struck key Saudi installations.
Against that backdrop, the visit by senior Saudi officials to Tehran stands out as a significant outreach at a time of profound tension between the two countries, with Saudi Arabia absorbing near-daily attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis. The kingdom was represented by Defence Minister Prince Khalid — the brother and trusted envoy of the crown prince.
His decision to travel to Iran under such conditions signalled that the Saudi leadership wants to avert another round of hostilities between the US, Israel and Iran, which could bring Iranian retaliatory strikes on American interests and installations in Saudi Arabia while the kingdom is still battling the Houthis.
For Iran, the presence of senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan has been symbolically important: Iranian officials are eager to sideline the US from regional security and diplomatic arrangements. Iran’s president expressed hope that the talks could help consolidate “regional unity and cohesion”.
For all the positivity, the central question remains whether the meeting could bridge the gap and help prevent a new round of US-Israeli aggression against Iran and, more importantly, de-escalate the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis.
No joint statement was issued, but individual comments since have been encouraging on the possibility of a broader regional security mechanism. Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, seemed satisfied after meeting officials from the three countries. “Very good discussions took place between us,” he told Iranian state television. “I feel that a new atmosphere is emerging in the region. … I sensed a very positive atmosphere in the discussions among the gentlemen.” Iranian officials are also hopeful that the meeting could be a prelude to further steps towards shaping “endogenous security — an issue that we have been insisting on for decades”.
    
The four countries have “agreed to continue discussions to strengthen cooperation … including on regional peace and security”. Indeed, the Tehran meeting was the most significant development yet that could help de-escalate the regional conflict. But the major question remains whether such emerging cooperation can prevent a fresh American-Israeli attack on Iran.
The reported reinforcement of American forces in the region, together with Israel’s continued genocidal war in Gaza and military action in Lebanon, poses the biggest threat to regional and global peace. The continued presence of American bases and troops in the Gulf countries has made their security far more vulnerable.
Most concerning is the escalating Saudi-Houthi conflict, which could trigger a wider conflagration and draw other countries into it. Iran could certainly play an important role in reaching a truce. The escalation could also hand Israel an opportunity to blunt resistance to its expansionist designs. Given Trump’s threatening rhetoric, there is a strong possibility that he will resume attacks on Iran after the midterm elections; the one thing that could stop him is the Republicans losing their majority in both the House and the Senate. And whatever the outcome of the Israeli general elections, there is no indication that the defeat of Netanyahu would change the policy of the Zionist state in any significant way. The divisions among regional countries give Israel complete impunity.
The quadrilateral meeting in Tehran and Iran’s positive response are certainly good omens. But the sources of tension remain that will not be easy to resolve, and the gap has yet to be bridged. It is vital that the Gulf countries refuse to let their soil be used for American aggression. Regional security can be ensured only through a regional security architecture. The Tehran meeting has provided an important opening for any such cooperation.
The writer is an author and journalist.

title: Rate hike
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE SBP’s decision to raise its policy rate by 50 basis points to 12pc was largely expected. It is also justified by growing risks to price stability. Although the increase has disappointed many businesses seeking cheaper credit, the monetary policy cannot be determined by their immediate financing needs. With global inflation proving stickier than expected, borrowing costs remaining high internationally, and domestic energy prices vulnerable to fresh external shocks, cutting or holding rates was no option. Pakistan’s recent currency stability, rising reserves and strong remittances have strengthened its external position. Still, these gains do not insulate the economy from the shocks of the Gulf war, or from tighter global financial conditions. Competition for capital is intensifying as major central banks tighten monetary policy, while the IMF expects global inflation to reach 4.7pc.
In this environment, the SBP must guard against entrenched inflation expectations and potential pressure on the rupee. Currency stability, achieved partly through subdued imports, cannot be treated as evidence that external vulnerabilities have disappeared. An abrupt increase in import demand, a rise in energy prices or tighter global financial conditions could quickly expose those weaknesses. The hike is a precaution against losing the gains made so far. Foreign investors have welcomed the hike, viewing it as necessary to contain inflation and safeguard macroeconomic stability amid global energy risks. However, trade bodies argue that inflation is driven by supply constraints, energy costs and fiscal distortions rather than excessive demand. Industry associations have similarly warned that expensive credit could force already struggling factories to cut production or shelve expansion plans. These concerns are legitimate. Industrial recovery remains fragile, and an extended period of expensive financing could weaken investment, employment and exports. But the answer is not to dismiss monetary tightening simply because it imposes costs. Tight money is no cure for supply-side inflationary pressures. But it keeps hard-won stability from slipping by anchoring expectations and protecting the rupee. The real relief for industry must come from lasting tax, power and regulatory reforms.

title: Trapped abroad
author: none@none.com (Rabiya Javeri Agha)
content:
FARID left his home in Narowal in search of a better future. A local agent charged him Rs800,000, promising him a well-paid job abroad. What awaited him, however, was nothing he could have imagined. For two years, he says, he was held in a prison-like compound near the Cambodia-Laos border. His passport had been confiscated, his movements were restricted, and his dreams shattered.
Farid’s job was to cook for hundreds of people who, like him, had been trafficked and trapped in scam centres. His working day began at 9am and continued until 4am, leaving him barely a few hours to rest. Any defiance was met with torture, including electric shocks. When authorities launched a crackdown on the scam centre, Farid managed to escape. But his freedom was short-lived as he was apprehended by Cambodian police and remains in a detention centre, waiting to return home.
Despite attempts to seek assistance through Pakistani diplomatic channels, Farid struggled to secure support. He approached the National Commission for Human Rights (NCHR) for help, but twice his return was held up by documentation requirements.
Farid’s story is not unique. In May 2026, the government informed the National Assembly of approximately 15,000 Pakistanis reportedly caught up in fraudulent employment schemes or in camps across Southeast Asia. As authorities have begun cracking down on these operations, thousands of Pakistanis now face difficulties returning home. Some need emergency travel documents, while others face penalties and bureaucratic delays. The same parents who struggled to finance their children’s journey abroad are now having to raise more money to bring them home.
We need to look more closely at recruitment networks.
Part of the difficulty is that those who have been trafficked are not always recognised as victims. Young people recruited in one country and forced to commit online fraud in another may themselves face arrest when these operations are raided. Their expired visas or confiscated passports become grounds for detention, while the deception and abuse they have suffered receive far less attention. Worse still, confiscated passports and identity documents may be misused by criminal networks to commit further fraud, potentially implicating victims in crimes they never committed. Even after escaping their traffickers, they stay behind bars, while those who exploited them often remain beyond the reach of the law.
Across its 2025 and 2026 investigations, Amnesty International identified nearly 100 scam compounds in Southeast Asia, documenting human trafficking, forced labour and torture. As authorities have begun raiding these operations, there are worrying signs that similar criminal networks are now taking root in other parts of the world, including Pakistan.
In August 2026, a raid on a suspected illegal call centre in Islamabad resulted in the detention of 500 foreign nationals, including Chinese and Vietnamese citizens. During a visit to Adiala Jail, we met approximately 70 women detained in connection with fraudulent activities.
Were they knowingly involved in fraud, or had some been deceived or coerced into working there? Online fraud is a serious crime and those responsible must be held accountable. But enforcement must distinguish between those who organise and profit from these operations and those who may themselves be victims of exploitation.
Pakistan already has institutions responsible for different aspects of call-centre operations. Yet many of them operate without registration, and there is insufficient monitoring to en­­su­­re that these establishments comply with the law.
A regularly upda­ted registry, coup­led with effective oversight, would help authorities distinguish between le­gitimate businesses and unregistered operations. We also need to look more closely at the recruitment networks operating within Pakistan. Who is offering these jobs? Who receives payment? And what action is taken when families report that someone has been trafficked abroad?
There must be closer coordination between cybercrime investigators, immigration authorities, anti-trafficking agencies and Pakistan’s diplomatic missions. Foreign nationals arrested in suspected scam operations should be screened for possible trafficking and provided with legal assistance. Pakistanis stranded abroad must have access to timely documentation and repatriation, including in countries without a resident embassy.
These are basic responsibilities of a government towards its citizens and towards people who may have been trafficked into its territory.
Farid is still waiting in Cambodia, having survived an experience no one should have to endure. It should not be so difficult to bring him home.
The writer is the chairperson of the National Commission for Human Rights.

title: Pakistan for all
author: none@none.com (Dr Niaz Murtaza)
content:
WHY haven’t we built a Pakistan where everyone enjoys equal rights? Postcolonial rulers in diverse countries had to build four basic pillars at once: capable states, dynamic economies, cohesive nations, and inclusive politics. Diversity, and in many cases inequalities and conflicts, made the last two vital so that diversity doesn’t mean divides.
But many ignored these subtle tasks to focus on the state and economy, only to make both non-inclusive. This led to conflicts that damaged states and economies. We did the same and faced the same fate. How can we now reverse gears? The answer is simple: ensure inclusive politics to produce a cohesive nation, which can create a capable state that can shape a dynamic economy, with each feeding the others in a virtuous circle. Are we creating this virtuous circle via inclusion or choking it via exclusion?
Inclusive politics needs a political culture where losers can bear losing electorally, knowing they will survive politically to aim for power again. But we have winner-takes-all, zero-sum politics rather than win-win politics — especially in the last four years as the PTI and nationalist parties in KP, Balochistan, and, more recently, Azad Kashmir face not just electoral defeat but also political extinction due to debatable judicial, electoral, and administrative manoeuvres. They are not seen as political rivals to defeat but existential enemies to eliminate. The imposition of emergency rule in KP is the latest such ploy.
Credible elections ensure broad ownership and support for tough decisions. Most of our elections have been controversial. The 2024 elections, in particular, are seen by many credible local and global analysts as having been blatantly rigged. Those elected freely must also be empowered fully once in power. In our case, informal power has long been wielded without accountability. But rarely have elected officials looked as clueless as today. The link between power and accountability to the public stands broken.
Inclusive politics produces a cohesive nation.
While opposing the unconstitutional usurpation of the powers of elected setups, inclusive politics also ensures constitutional checks and balances so that they don’t abuse power. This is done via the horizontal division of power across the executive, parliament, the judiciary, and electoral and accountability state bodies. While such division has always been weak in Pakistan, the boundaries among them have become so blurred in the last four years that the three main power organs look to some like a triumvirate.
Inclusive politics also divides power vertically among federal, provincial, and local setups. Such distribution gives different groups a chance to govern. Those who could not win federally in a given election or can never win there due to their limited support still have a chance to win power provincially or locally. It also brings rulers closer to people to make them more accountable. Concentrating power federally turns too many citizens into permanent losers and reduces accountability. But local bodies elections have not been held for long in most provinces and regions, and provinces have usurped the financial and administrative powers of even those in place. Provinces, in turn, face the same fate at the hands of the centre and some see plans to weaken them further by creating small provinces.
Inclusive politics also empowers individuals and civic groups to criticise elected setups by giving them a wide range of freedoms and rights. But they have been severely curtailed. HRCP’s last annual report des­cri­bes growing curbs on free speech and hu­­man rights. Journa­li­sts, political workers, lawyers, and activists face flimsy cases un­­der draconian cybercrime, sedition, and antiterrorism laws. Threats and disappearances make speaking out dangerous.
Instead of reversing gears, we are actually accelerating on the current self-destructive path. The dream of a Pakistan for everyone has given way to a grim reality of a country for a handful of people who monopolise power and wealth.
Rulers are gaining power but losing legitimacy and trust. Exclusion rather than inclusion, and coercion rather than consent prevail.
The state is struggling to end the violence its past policies helped create, while its current policies risk fuelling violence. A secure state can’t emerge from a divided nation, nor can an economy thrive on exclusion. The inclusionary pillars we neglect will keep weakening the exclusionary pillars we build. With inclusive politics nowhere in sight, a cohesive nation, a capable state and a dynamic economy will remain a pipe dream.
The writer has a PhD degree in political economy from the University of California, Berkeley, and 25 years of grassroots to senior-level experience across 50 countries.

title: Dengue season
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
ANOTHER dengue outbreak looms over the country for reasons of lack of preparedness and negligence. This month’s caseload of the disease continues to surge in KP, with 51 new incidents reported on Sunday. The provincial tally now stands at 4,856. October is the time of year when dengue hits its highest point. According to a report by IDRS at the Directorate General Health Services of KP, as many as 2,244 cases were recorded in the current month. The maximum number of infections was in Kohat: out of a total of 2,822 cases as many as 1,230 form this month’s tally. Not only do these figures lay bare the systemic rot in the health infrastructure, but KP’s virus burden has set the alarm bells ringing in the rest of the country. Last year, the Sindh High Court reprimanded senior health officials for gross incompetence as procurement disputes led to a scarcity of testing kits and it took public fury for fumigation drives to start. Despite cooler weather, Punjab’s hospitals too were inundated with patients. Meanwhile, our underreporting levels are shocking. Most patients either opt for home isolation or go to private clinics and laboratories. This excludes them from official data, rendering the government’s response haphazard and reactive.
In unpredictable climate conditions, official lethargy cannot persist. High humidity and unexpectedly warm temperatures mean a prolonged breeding season for mosquitoes. Moreover, heavy rains and broken drainage only exacerbate the crisis. Additionally, the fact that patients take longer to recover indicates that a more lethal and resistant strain is among us. The authorities must ensure transparent and updated data, prompt management, and most importantly, advance prevention mechanisms. Citizens should not face preventable misery. Cohesive surveillance systems that cover private facilities, testing kits, and adequate knowledge about ever-evolving viral strains are overdue. What was once mild seasonal discomfort has morphed into an all-year public health emergency due to institutional apathy.

title: Privatisation framework
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE proposed merger of the Privatisation Commission and the Public-Private Partnership Authority (P3A) into a single institution is a sensible move. It will end the duality of functions and provide a more coherent framework for mobilising private capital to manage public assets and develop physical infrastructure for which the state has limited resources to spare. Although the two bodies operate under separate laws, their mandates intersect in bringing private capital and expertise into areas dominated by the state. A unified entity could offer a common platform for evaluating these options.
Privatisation involves transferring ownership or control of state assets, while public-private partnerships (PPPs) allow governments to enlist private capital for projects they cannot finance. Both approaches require sound financial assessments and clear risk allocations. With Pakistan facing persistent fiscal constraints, the state cannot afford to finance loss-making enterprises indefinitely. Private investment can help ease these pressures, but it is not an end in itself. Poorly structured transactions can leave the state with inadequate returns or costly contractual obligations. The proposed legislation envisages four public funds to support privatisation and PPP transactions. These instruments could help prepare viable projects and attract investment. However, they must not become vehicles for subsidising commercially unsound ventures. Government guarantees and liabilities should be disclosed and assessed before deals are approved. The proposed legal protections for serving and former officials acting in good faith also require careful rethinking. Officials should be protected against frivolous litigation when making decisions in the public interest. Such protection must not, however, become immunity from accountability. Making PPP agreements accessible as public documents is also positive. Public scrutiny is particularly important when private investors enter long-term arrangements that may impose financial obligations on taxpayers and successive governments.
The new arrangement offers an opportunity to improve the management of state assets and infrastructure investment. Its success will depend on securing fair value for public property, attracting credible investors and ensuring that partnerships deliver tangible benefits. The bill proposes a majority-independent board with private-sector representation to strengthen commercial decision-making. Its effectiveness will require transparent appointments, relevant expertise, political independence, clear performance benchmarks, strong accountability, and enforceable conflict-of-interest rules to ensure effective governance. The state must now ensure that commercial discipline, transparency and accountability guide its implementation.

title: Whither terrorism
author: none@none.com (Arifa Noor)
content:
THE future of Khyber Pakhtun­khwa remains unclear, whether it’s as a single entity or as a democratic one. PTI, we are told, has been made PNG — once again. And the south of KP is reportedly being carved out rapidly to be a new province or to simply reverse the amendment that made the former Fata part of KP. No one is really sure what the coming days hold.
Amid this confusion, a newly appointed member of the Area Representative and Development Council (ARDC) for the special emergency-hit districts of the south has created another storm in a teacup. In a video statement he spoke of reaching out to the Afghan Taliban to bring peace to Pakistan. Considering that this preference for dialogue over conflict with the fitna-across-the-border ostensibly has been the reason the PTI government was sent home, a similar message of love from the new advisory council just wasn’t cricket. But before we could get our breath back at this audacity, the new spokesman of the region, Mehmood Jan Babar, added to the mess by not denying the idea altogether.
Eventually Samar Bilour, who represents the Peshawar-led advisory council, had to enter the fray to diss the notion of talks. As an aside, we now have a Peshawar council and a Southern council.
    
Be that as it may, the point is these statements have simply added to the confusion surrounding the province. And terrorism, despite the frequency of the attacks and the statements of the government, has taken a backseat.
The focus is more on what the grand plan for KP is. Is it simply to close the doors on PTI? Is it to conduct an experiment on the efficacy of newer, smaller provinces? Or is it simply to reverse the Fata merger? Or perhaps it was to give the governor the chance to clear encroachments, a favourite problem for most non-elected officials these days. As the Urdu saying goes, there are as many rumours as there are mouths.
We appear to be using the same old playbook put together in the post-Musharraf period.
But none of these rumours seem to be highlighting the basic issue — how to address the decades-old problem of militancy in these regions. Other than vague promises of fighting the problem, there is little that has been shared with the people to explain what the new government is doing or planning to do.
And this is where the problem lies.
Militancy is going from bad to worse. The intensity of the attacks is worrying and impacts the entire country, especially one looking for more foreign investment. But while the state is clear on its decision to fight its way to victory, it doesn’t seem to have a clear strategy or path for this — or so it appears to those on the outside.
Any strategy to succeed must take into account the current environment.
However, we appear to be using the same old playbook put together in the post-Musharraf period when the TTP was controlling large swathes of land in what is now former Fata. In order to flush the Taliban out, military operations were conducted after the ordinary residents were persuaded to leave their homes and villages before the clearing out was done. And once the area/s were cleared, the displaced people were allowed to return to their homes and businesses.
However, nearly two decades later, the TTP is no longer controlling areas; it seems to appear only to conduct attacks or block roads, or carry out other activities and then melt away. And yet, it seems, our strategy remains the same — of wanting to clear out areas, be it at the level of villages and so on.
But if the TTP is not controlling these areas and the plan is to clear out the residents before launching operations, surely the TTP will also vacate the areas along with the residents and simply return later. How is this effective? And this is all the more difficult now because 20 years earlier, the TTP escaped to an Afghanistan run by a hostile government, which is no longer the case. But these questions are really not being discussed.
The intelligence-based operations (IBOs) are also offered as an alternative. Though once again, there is little clarity on how effective these are; they only become public when they lead to deaths of troops, which is tragic. But once again, there is little information available on why there is even one fatality during an IBO. And if they are effective, then why has the problem simply grown?
    
The second problem with this strategy is the public sentiment, which is against military operations because of the displacement and suffering that comes in the wake of this. But more than that, the displacements were not accompanied by the compensation the people had been promised — for the damage to their property and business. This has been a major reason for their reluctance to support operations this time around. And yet, this also does not seem to have led to any kind of brainstorming about what to do differently.
More worrying still is the distrust or alienation of the people in general from the state as well as the TTP. In many anecdotal accounts, it is suggested the local residents of the affected areas see the activities of the TTP and the state as alienating. These gaps with the state, ideally, should be bridged before operations are launched. It is rather obvious that kinetic operations cannot succeed without the people’s support. And yet the state seems to be doing little to earn this support or trust.
And along with all this comes the larger issue of why the kinetic operations, whenever they have succeeded, are not followed by a successful handover to strong functioning civilian institutions which can then govern effectively. In other words, the build-and-transfer part has eluded us for decades.
Indeed, the reduction of the debate over terrorism to a simple one of using force or not is a very one-dimensional one. The problem requires a lot more depth and nuance than is realised.
The writer is a journalist.
Published in Dawn, October 27th, 2026

Public sentiment is largely against military operations due to unfulfilled promises of compensation for displacement and damage, leading to distrust and alienation from both the state and the TTP, undermining the potential for kinetic success.

A significant gap exists in the 'build-and-transfer' mechanism, where successful kinetic operations are not followed by the establishment of strong, functioning civilian institutions to ensure long-term governance and stability.

title: AI agenda
author: none@none.com (Huma Yusuf)
content:
WHEN asked what he would dress up as for Halloween, a 10-year-old boy I know responded, “Claude, because there’s nothing scarier than AI.” Whether you consider this funny or astute, it highlights the pervasiveness of the AI bogeyman. And the best thing to do with your fears is face them.
So it was good to see Pakistan play a prominent role at the recent Global Digital and AI Summit in Seoul and ramp up engagement with the World Bank to support the country’s digital transformation through a Digital and AI Compact. Pakistan has committed to spending $1 billion on AI by 2030 and is cracking on with plans to digitise 12 key sectors by 2035 under the National Digital Master Plan.
As the momentum builds, we must ask: how will Pakistan fund investment in AI? And what makes digital transformation and AI adoption capable of overcoming structural issues that have held back traditional activities like manufacturing?
AI use — particularly localised AI development and large language model (LLM) training — requires an immense and stable energy supply, high-speed internet and data storage, none of which are readily available in Pakistan. While efforts are underway to boost 5G spectrum and satellite access, the electricity sector is plagued by outages, a dilapidated grid, and circular debt. Concerns abound about whether Pakistan’s scarce water supply can bear the burden of water-guzzling data centres.
Then there’s the question of how to insulate the future of Pakistani youth from widespread AI adoption. Pakistan’s first economic census last year identified that the services sector makes up over 50 per cent of the country’s economy (production is less than 30pc).
How will Pakistan fund investment into AI?
A recent World Bank report notes that the services sector is most vulnerable to AI adoption, with 61pc of Pakistani service workers in jobs with higher-than-average AI exposure. Based on 2024 data, the report indicates that 8pc of all jobs are at risk of being replaced by AI (a number likely to rise). This means many Pakistanis will be trapped in low-skill, low-paying, and climate-vulnerable agricultural or manual labour jobs, while a sliver of society benefits from productivity gains.
The other question is how to prevent the complete securitisation of the AI agenda, a common challenge in countries with national security preoccupations. Concerns about the use of LLMs for mass surveillance have been voiced in the US and China, a scenario that Pakistan, with its punitive electronic crime legislation, is well primed for. Early interest has also been expressed in using AI for smart policing and biometric identity management. An early, advanced data centre was built under a National Aerospace Science and Technology Park initiative. 
The state will feel a growing need to direct AI investment towards national security, because it’s only a matter of time before local terrorist groups begin deploying AI in anti-state activities. Writing in South Asian Voices, Zohaib Altaf and Nimrah Javed highlight the risk of such groups using AI to better target attacks based on intelligence analysis or to support arms development, particularly weaponised drones. The precedent for this has already been set by the Houthis in Yemen, so the likelihood of AI investment being funnelled primarily to military ends is high.
If Pakistan’s AI agenda is not carefully monitored, we face a future in which limited digital infrastructure in the form of resource-intensive data centres is reserved for security-linked AI use, with some private enterprises enjoying gains at the expense of the wider population. In this scenario, urban youth unemployment increases and rural poverty intensifies; agricultural emp­l­o­yment survives the AI rollout, but is ravaged by climate change instead.
There is a way to prevent this scenario. That’s through high levels of transparency and accountability in AI governance, regulation, and investment, including the requirement for public service considerations and consultation as part of all investments. Pakistan’s civil society organisations and media should also redouble efforts to understand the implications of AI investment to ensure accountability.
On a more positive note, the notions of accountability and transparency in AI are no longer antithetical to AI development. US-based civic activism against data centres on resource-use grounds is increasingly effective in blocking projects. And while Big Tech has thrown up its hands, arguing that it can’t be held responsible for what LLMs do, new research suggests that LLMs may be easier to unpick (and so monitor) than we think. Such public-interest considerations, particularly with an inclusion lens, should be part of Pakistan’s AI journey. That may make it less scary. 
The writer is a political and integrity risk analyst.
